title: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Few living species will leave descendants; common species of dominant groups will prevail

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Very few living species will leave descendants in the far future, and those that will prevail and give rise to new dominant species will be the common, widespread species of the larger, dominant groups.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: We can so far take a prophetic glance into futurity as to foretel that it will be the common and widely-spread species, belonging to the larger and dominant groups, which will ultimately prevail and procreate new and dominant species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion”; section “Concluding remarks”. Scope: living species and their future descendants (testable retrospectively in the fossil record)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch14-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Retrospective fossil cohorts can test close analogues of the prediction. They cannot literally resolve the future fate of present species, and genealogical descent is often uncertain.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In fossil intervals, treat species present at an earlier time as the prediction cohort and test whether initially common, widespread species in species-rich clades disproportionately persist or give rise to later diversity. Low descendant survival overall and positive effects of abundance, range and clade dominance support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Direct ancestor-descendant links are rarely known.

Observed abundance and range are highly sampling-dependent.

The far future of living species is not directly testable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The future-looking sentence has a clear retrospective translation, and fossil occurrences record occupancy, clade size and which taxa persist. That translation is a proxy, and sampling bias toward widespread genera is severe enough to limit discriminating power. The survivorship model itself is a standard paleobiological analysis that can be run on existing downloads.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: At successive fossil time slices, score which species or genera still have descendants several intervals later, and test whether survivorship and later diversification are concentrated in taxa that were common, widespread and members of already large groups. The claim is confirmed if those traits predict leaving descendants and most taxa leave none, and refuted if rare members of small groups persist as often as common members of dominant groups.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
True species-level ancestor-descendant links are usually unavailable, so the test is forced down to genus occupancy.

Later geological intervals are a proxy for the 'far future', and the length of that proxy changes the result.

Widespread taxa are more likely to be collected again, which imitates higher survivorship.

data adequacy: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.7
